title: Jurassic Park
wiki_lead:
Jurassic Park is a 1993 American science fiction film directed by Steven Spielberg and written by Michael Crichton and David Koepp, based on Crichton's 1990 novel of the same name. Starring Sam Neill, Laura Dern, Jeff Goldblum, and Richard Attenborough, the film follows a group of visitors struggling to survive after sabotage disables the security systems of a dinosaur theme park, releasing the dinosaurs.
Spielberg acquired the film rights before the novel's publication for $1.5 million through Universal Pictures, with Crichton receiving an additional $500,000 to adapt the story. David Koepp wrote the final screenplay, streamlining the novel and revising several characters. Filming took place in California and Hawaii from August to November 1992, followed by post-production through May 1993. The dinosaurs were created using computer-generated imagery by Industrial Light & Magic and animatronics by Stan Winston's team. Spielberg also invested in DTS to support the film's digital surround sound. Its release was accompanied by a $65 million marketing campaign involving more than 100 licensing partners.
Jurassic Park premiered in Washington, D.C., on June 9, 1993, and was released in the United States two days later. It grossed over $914 million during its original theatrical run, surpassing E.T. the Extra-Terrestrial to become the highest-grossing film of all time until the release of Titanic. The film received critical acclaim for its visual effects, sound design, action sequences, John Williams's score, and Spielberg's direction. It won three Academy Awards for sound effects editing, sound, and visual effects. Following its 20th anniversary re-release in 2013, its worldwide box-office total surpassed $1 billion.
Since its release, many film critics and industry professionals have regarded Jurassic Park as one of the greatest films ever made. Its groundbreaking use of computer-generated imagery is widely seen as a turning point that shaped the visual effects techniques used in modern cinema. In 2018, the Library of Congress selected Jurassic Park for preservation in the United States National Film Registry as "culturally, historically, or aesthetically significant". The film spawned a multimedia franchise that includes six sequels, starting with The Lost World: Jurassic Park, as well as a variety of other media.

Plot
Industrialist John Hammond has created Jurassic Park, an animal theme park featuring de-extinct dinosaurs, on the tropical island Isla Nublar, off the coast of Costa Rica. After a Velociraptor kills a dinosaur handler, the park's investors, represented by lawyer Donald Gennaro, threaten to pull funding unless experts certify the island's safety. Gennaro invites the chaotician Ian Malcolm, while Hammond invites the paleontologist Alan Grant and the paleobotanist Ellie Sattler. grok_lead: Jurassic Park, later rebranded as Jurassic World, is an American science fiction adventure media franchise created by author Michael Crichton and produced primarily by Universal Pictures, revolving around the development and disastrous operation of a theme park featuring dinosaurs cloned from prehistoric DNA on the fictional Isla Nublar island off Costa Rica. The franchise originated with Crichton's techno-thriller novel Jurassic Park, published in November 1990 by Alfred A. Knopf, which follows a team of genetic scientists who clone dinosaurs using ancient DNA extracted from mosquitoes preserved in amber, only for the park's security systems to fail, unleashing the creatures on visitors including a paleontologist, mathematician, and lawyer. The novel explores themes of bioethics, chaos theory, and the perils of unchecked scientific ambition, becoming a bestseller with over 416 pages and a cover price of $32.50. In 1993, Universal Pictures adapted the novel into a blockbuster film directed by Steven Spielberg, starring Sam Neill, Laura Dern, Jeff Goldblum, and Richard Attenborough, which depicts experts touring the park in June 1993 before a tropical storm and sabotage over the weekend of June 11â12 lead to deadly dinosaur attacks, including by Tyrannosaurus rex and Velociraptors. The film, co-written by Crichton and David Koepp, revolutionized visual effects with groundbreaking CGI dinosaurs created by Industrial Light & Magic, grossing $1,058,454,230 worldwide and earning three Academy Awards for sound, visual effects, and editing. The franchise expanded with five sequels: The Lost World: Jurassic Park (1997), directed by Spielberg and grossing $618,638,999 worldwide, focusing on a second island expedition and corporate exploitation; Jurassic Park III (2001), directed by Joe Johnston and earning $365,900,000, involving a search for a missing boy on Isla Sorna; Jurassic World (2015), directed by Colin Trevorrow and achieving $1,671,063,641 worldwide as the franchise's highest-grosser, reopening the park with hybrid dinosaur s; Jurassic World: Fallen Kingdom (2018), directed by J.A. Bayona and grossing $1,308,323,302, dealing with a volcanic eruption and dinosaur auctions; and Jurassic World: Dominion (2022), directed by Trevorrow and earning $1,004,004,592, uniting human and dinosaur worlds amid genetic threats. The most recent installment, Jurassic World Rebirth (2025), directed by Gareth Edwards, follows an extraction mission to the original facility and has grossed $868,613,830 worldwide. Cumulatively, the six main films have generated $6,895,204,381 in worldwide box office revenue as of November 2025, making it one of the highest-grossing franchises in cinematic history. Beyond films, the franchise includes Crichton's sequel novel The Lost World (1995), comic books, video games, and extensive merchandising, but its most notable extensions are immersive theme park attractions at Universal destinations. Universal Orlando Resort features Jurassic World VelociCoaster, a high-speed roller coaster, Jurassic Park River Adventure, a water ride with animatronic dinosaur s, and the interactive Jurassic Park Discovery Center. Similar experiences exist at Universal Studios Hollywood with Jurassic World â The Ride, a boat-based attraction showcasing a Mosasaurus feeding, and at Universal Studios Japan with Jurassic Park: The Ride. These attractions, operational since 1996 in various forms, have drawn millions by recreating the franchise's perilous dinosaur encounters.
